newsitem.title: THAILAND: Brokers upset as foreign Thai stocks players hit.
newsitem.headline: Brokers upset as foreign Thai stocks players hit.

text.p: Brokers expressed frustration on Tuesday as Thai authorities moved unexpectedly to stop foreign players from raising much-needed baht through stock sales on the local bourse.

In an unprecedented move, the Securities and Exchange Commission, which regulates the stock market, said all foreigners would be temporarily required by the central bank to settle their stocks trades in U.S. dollars only.
The Bank of Thailand said separately it would ask institutions providing custodian services not to transfer unpaid stocks to foreign accounts.
Analysts said the central bank move could help slow the selling of Thai stocks by foreign investors who had resorted to short sales of stocks to raise baht funds.
"There is a complete uneasiness. This is quite negative," said one analyst at a foreign brokerage.
"(Foreign) investors are even more concerned that whatever they do here, it is not very good for business because authorities can change regulations anytime they want," he said.

Some foreigners were said by brokers to have been selling Thai stocks heavily from last week to raise baht to cover their squeezed short positions in the forex market after last month's speculative attack on the Thai unit.
Their sales to raise baht came after the central bank effectively cut off local sources of supply through capital controls last month, analysts said.

Central bank measures to cut off baht supply to foreign speculators have resulted in an informal two-tier baht market -- offshore and onshore -- and caused the value of the baht to rocket last week to a 13-year-high in the offshore market.

"There would be some side-effect from the central bank's recent move to cut baht supply through the stock market. Activities in the market (by foreigners) would be reduced," said Kasem Prunratanamala, an analyst at HSBC James Capel.
"There will also be some psychological effect as investors are concerned about the possibility of more new measures in the future," he said.
The head of a U.S. investment bank said the new measures showed that Thai authorities were determined to punish currency speculators and cut off any access to funds to them.
"Clearly Thailand is going through some very rough times and will do anything to fight off speculators," he added.
Other analysts said the Thai bourse, which is floundering at an eight-year low, could dive further with the introduction of the new restrictive measures.
The Singapore-based research house I.D.E.A. said foreign players might have sold off Thai stocks to acquire much-needed baht and to bail out of the tumbling bourse.

"Of course, this intention (to cash out of Thai stocks) will merely send the benchmark SET Index to the 500-target much earlier than expected, thereby defeating all efforts by the authorities to prop up the ailing stock market," it said.

Other analysts said the change in rules for foreigner transactions could result in defaults if some players had not made prior arrangements to maintain funds in U.S. dollars to make settlement or were unable to raise such funds in time.
On the other hand, it could also spark another major scramble by foreigners for baht and drive up offshore baht rates to new highs, they added.
The baht rose again in the offshore market late on Tuesday to 23.900 following the new measures, after being calm in the past few days.
